questions.stem: Which statement about the enzymes and DNA synthesis at a bacterial replication fork is correct?
options: Helicase synthesises the short RNA primers needed to start DNA synthesis.
DNA polymerase can begin synthesis of a new strand without needing a primer.
DNA ligase unwinds the parental double helix ahead of the replication fork.
The leading strand is synthesised continuously from a single primer, while the lagging strand is synthesised in short fragments as the fork opens.
The leading strand requires a new primer for each fragment it synthesises.
questions.exp: Helicase unwinds the parental double helix, primase lays down the RNA primers, DNA polymerase can only extend an existing primer, and ligase seals the gaps between fragments. Only the lagging strand, which grows away from the opening fork, needs a series of primers and fragments; the leading strand is continuous from a single primer.

questions.stem: Which statement about transcription in a eukaryotic cell is correct?
options: Transcription begins when RNA polymerase binds to the terminator sequence of a gene.
RNA polymerase synthesises the new RNA strand in the 3' to 5' direction.
RNA polymerase requires an RNA primer before it can start copying a gene.
The poly-A tail is a stretch of DNA sequence copied from the end of the gene.
RNA polymerase binds to the promoter and starts RNA synthesis without a primer, using one DNA strand as a template.
questions.exp: RNA polymerase recognises the promoter and starts RNA synthesis without a primer, unlike DNA polymerase. RNA is made in the 5' to 3' direction, the terminator is the stop signal for transcription, and the poly-A tail is added enzymatically to the finished pre-mRNA in the nucleus.

questions.stem: Which statement about the ribosome during translation is correct?
options: A tRNA carrying the next amino acid enters at the A site, where its anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon.
The growing polypeptide chain is carried on a tRNA sitting in the A site while new tRNAs enter at the P site.
The E site is where peptide bonds are formed between amino acids.
The initiator tRNA binds first to the A site of the ribosome when translation starts.
In eukaryotes, ribosomes begin translating an mRNA while that mRNA is still being transcribed.
questions.exp: A charged tRNA enters at the A site, moves to the P site as the chain grows, and leaves at the E site. The initiator tRNA begins in the P site, peptide bonds form at the peptidyl transferase centre of the large subunit, and simultaneous transcription and translation is a prokaryotic feature.

questions.stem: The beginning of an mRNA reads 5' AUG GCA UAC GGU UAA 3', where AUG is the start codon and UAA is a stop codon. Codon meanings: AUG = methionine, GCA = alanine, GCC = alanine, GUA = valine, UAC = tyrosine, GGU = glycine, CGG = arginine, UUA = leucine. Two independent mutations occur in different copies of this gene. Mutation 1 substitutes one base so that codon 2 reads GCC instead of GCA. Mutation 2 inserts a single G immediately after codon 2. Which statement about the resulting proteins is correct?
options: Both mutations are silent, because neither changes any amino acid in the protein.

Mutation 1 is silent, while mutation 2 shifts the reading frame, so from codon 3 onward the mRNA reads GUA, CGG and UUA instead of UAC, GGU and UAA, changing the amino acids and losing the stop codon.
Mutation 1 is silent and mutation 2 changes only the amino acid encoded by codon 2.
Mutation 1 changes the amino acid at position 2 of the protein, while mutation 2 is silent.
Mutation 2 adds exactly one extra amino acid to the protein and leaves all the other amino acids unchanged.
questions.exp: GCA and GCC both code for alanine, so mutation 1 is silent. The inserted base shifts the reading frame: from codon 3 the mRNA specifies valine and arginine where tyrosine and glycine were, and the stop codon becomes a codon for leucine, so translation would continue past it.

questions.stem: In a testcross, a pea plant heterozygous for three independently assorting genes, AaBbCc, is crossed with a plant that is aabbcc. What is the probability that an offspring is heterozygous at all three loci (AaBbCc)?
questions.exp: At each locus the cross is Aa with aa, which gives heterozygous and homozygous recessive offspring in equal proportions, so the chance of heterozygous is 1/2. The three genes assort independently, so the probabilities multiply: 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8.

questions.stem: Cystic fibrosis is caused by an autosomal recessive allele. Two parents without the condition have one child with cystic fibrosis and a second child who is healthy. What is the probability that this healthy second child is a carrier of the allele?
questions.exp: The affected child shows that both parents are heterozygous carriers. Among their healthy children the genotypes occur in the ratio 1 AA to 2 Aa, because aa individuals are affected, so the probability that a healthy child is a carrier is 2 out of 3.

questions.stem: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A woman has no symptoms, but her father had haemophilia. She and her husband, who does not have haemophilia, are expecting their first child. What is the probability that the first child is a daughter who carries the allele?
questions.exp: The woman received her father's only X chromosome, which carried the allele, so she is a carrier. The chance the first child is a girl is 1/2, and a girl of a carrier mother and an unaffected father has a 1/2 chance of being a carrier: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.stem: In a series of crosses, the recombination frequencies between three linked genes are: between gene a and gene b, 4 percent; between gene b and gene c, 9 percent; between gene a and gene c, 13 percent. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The genes are arranged with gene b between the other two, in the order a b c.
The genes are arranged with gene a between the other two, in the order b a c.
The genes are arranged with gene c between the other two, in the order a c b.
No valid order exists, because the recombination frequency between two genes must be the same whichever third gene is considered.
The three genes must lie on three different chromosomes.
questions.exp: The largest distance, 13 percent, equals the sum of the other two, 4 + 9, so the two shorter intervals lie side by side with gene b in the middle. Genes on different chromosomes would show recombination frequencies close to 50 percent.

questions.stem: Which event occurs during anaphase of mitosis in an animal cell?
options: Homologous chromosome pairs separate and move to opposite poles.
Chromosomes align along the equator of the cell.
The nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle begins to form.
Nuclear envelopes re-form around each group of chromosomes.
Sister chromatids separate at the centromeres and move toward opposite poles.
questions.exp: Anaphase of mitosis begins when sister chromatids split at the centromere and are pulled to opposite poles by the spindle. Homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I of meiosis; the other events belong to metaphase, prophase and telophase.

questions.stem: During meiosis II in a human oocyte, the sister chromatids of chromosome 21 fail to separate, while meiosis I and the rest of meiosis II proceed normally. One of the resulting egg cells receives both copies of chromosome 21 and is then fertilised by a normal sperm. Which statement is correct?
options: The zygote has 46 chromosomes and is chromosomally normal.
The zygote has 45 chromosomes, with only one copy of chromosome 21.
The zygote has 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21, the condition known as Down syndrome.
The zygote has 69 chromosomes because all chromosomes are present in triplicate.
The zygote has 47 chromosomes, but the extra chromosome is a sex chromosome.
questions.exp: Nondisjunction of sister chromatids in meiosis II produces one egg with both copies of chromosome 21 (n + 1) and one with none. Fertilisation of the n + 1 egg by a normal sperm gives 47 chromosomes with three copies of chromosome 21, the karyotype of Down syndrome.

questions.stem: Before industrialisation, light coloured peppered moths rested on pale, lichen covered tree trunks and greatly outnumbered dark coloured moths. As industrial soot blackened the trunks, the dark form became far more common within a few decades. Which statement best explains this change?
options: Individual moths gradually darkened during their own lifetimes as soot settled on the trees.

The dark form arose by random mutation before the trunks darkened; once the trunks became dark, birds caught more light moths, so dark moths survived and reproduced more successfully and passed on their alleles.
Soot chemically altered the genes of the moths so that their offspring were born dark.
The moths sensed the darkening trunks and produced dark offspring in order to blend into the background.
Dark coloured moths were already more common than light moths before the trees darkened.
questions.exp: Variation from random mutation existed before selection acted on it. The change in the environment altered the selection pressure: on dark trunks light moths were more visible to predatory birds, so the better camouflaged dark morph survived and reproduced more. The other options describe acquired characteristics or directed change, which natural selection does not involve.

questions.stem: A population of diploid flowering plants grows in one meadow with no physical barriers. A mutation arises in one lineage that doubles the chromosome number, producing tetraploid plants. Tetraploids mate successfully with other tetraploids, but crosses between tetraploid and diploid plants produce seeds that die before germination. Which statement is correct?
options: This is allopatric speciation, because the tetraploid and diploid plants cannot interbreed.
This is sympatric speciation: a reproductively isolated polyploid lineage has formed within the same geographic area.
No speciation can occur without a physical barrier such as a river or a mountain range.
The tetraploid and diploid plants still belong to one biological species, because they live in the same meadow.
A change in chromosome number can alter gene expression but can never give rise to a new species.
questions.exp: Sympatric speciation occurs without geographic separation, and polyploidy is a well known mechanism of it in plants. Because tetraploid crosses with diploids fail, the tetraploid lineage is reproductively isolated from the diploids even though both grow side by side, which satisfies the biological species criterion.

questions.stem: Which statement about the role of water in the light dependent reactions of photosynthesis is correct?
options: The oxygen released by photosynthesis comes from water molecules split during the light dependent reactions.
The oxygen released by photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide that is split in the thylakoid membranes.
Electrons released by the splitting of water are passed directly to photosystem I to replace its lost electrons.
Water is split in the stroma as part of the Calvin cycle.
The splitting of water directly produces the ATP that the Calvin cycle consumes.
questions.exp: Photolysis of water occurs at photosystem II in the thylakoid membranes: the electrons released replace those that photosystem II loses to the electron transport chain, and the oxygen atoms are released as O2. ATP is generated by chemiosmosis, and carbon dioxide is fixed later in the Calvin cycle in the stroma.

questions.stem: Which statement about long distance transport in flowering plants is correct?
options: Xylem transports sugars from the leaves to the roots, while phloem transports water and mineral ions upward.
The contents of both xylem and phloem are moved mainly by the transpiration pull from the leaves.
Mature xylem vessels consist of living cells that actively pump water from cell to cell.
Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral ions upward from the roots, while phloem transports sugars from source tissues to sink tissues.
Phloem can transport sugars only downward, from the leaves to the roots.
questions.exp: Xylem carries water and mineral ions upward in dead, hollow vessel elements, driven by transpiration pull. Phloem moves sucrose from sources such as mature leaves to sinks such as roots, fruits and growing buds, in living sieve tube elements, and the flow can go upward or downward.

questions.stem: In a healthy heart, the ventricles begin to contract shortly after the atria contract. Which statement explains this timing?
options: The atria and the ventricles are excited at the same moment, but ventricular muscle contracts more slowly than atrial muscle.
The delay is caused by the time blood takes to flow from the atria into the ventricles.
A second impulse from the sinoatrial node travels directly to the ventricles and triggers their contraction.

The impulse from the sinoatrial node is delayed at the atrioventricular node, so the ventricles are excited shortly after the atria, allowing the atria to finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
The ventricles contract first and the atria contract during the diastole that follows.
questions.exp: The impulse from the sinoatrial node spreads across the atrial muscle and is held up briefly at the atrioventricular node before travelling through the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres to the ventricles. This delay in the conduction pathway lets atrial systole fill the ventricles before ventricular systole begins; it is not caused by the speed of blood flow or by different muscle speeds.

questions.stem: Which statement about ultrafiltration at the glomerulus is correct?
options: Fluid is forced from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule by blood pressure, and the filtrate normally contains glucose, urea and ions but no plasma proteins or blood cells.
Plasma proteins pass freely into the filtrate and are reabsorbed later along the loop of Henle.
Glucose is actively transported from the blood into the filtrate at the glomerulus.
Red blood cells normally enter the filtrate and are returned to the blood in the distal tubule.
Water is moved out of the glomerular capillaries by active transport.
questions.exp: High hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries forces water and small solutes such as glucose, amino acids, urea and ions through the filtration membranes. Plasma proteins and blood cells are too large to pass and remain in the blood. Glucose returns to the blood by reabsorption in the proximal tubule, not by secretion into the filtrate.

questions.stem: Which statement about nerve action potentials is correct?
options: A stronger stimulus produces a single action potential with a larger amplitude.
Subthreshold stimuli produce small action potentials that travel more slowly along the axon.
Once threshold is reached, the amplitude of the action potential is fixed; a stronger stimulus increases the frequency of action potentials, not their size.
The refractory period allows action potentials to travel backwards along the axon as well as forwards.
During repolarisation, the inside of the axon becomes even more positive than at the peak of depolarisation.
questions.exp: The action potential is an all or none event: every impulse above threshold has the same amplitude, and stimulus strength is encoded by the frequency of firing. Subthreshold stimuli produce no action potential at all, the refractory period ensures one way propagation, and repolarisation returns the membrane potential toward negative values.

questions.stem: Which statement about the control of cortisol secretion is correct?
options: Cortisol is released by the adrenal medulla in response to nerve signals from the hypothalamus.
When cortisol levels fall, the anterior pituitary releases less ACTH so that cortisol stays low.
Cortisol raises its own secretion through a positive feedback loop.
ACTH travels down nerve fibres from the hypothalamus to the adrenal cortex.
A rise in blood cortisol acts by negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, reducing the release of CRH and ACTH.
questions.exp: The hypothalamus releases CRH, the anterior pituitary responds by releasing ACTH into the blood, and ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol. Rising cortisol then suppresses both CRH and ACTH release, a negative feedback loop that keeps cortisol within set limits.

questions.stem: Which statement about B and T lymphocytes is correct?
options: B lymphocytes mature in the thymus before circulating in the blood.
Activated B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies, whereas cytotoxic T cells destroy infected body cells by direct contact.
T lymphocytes are the main antibody secreting cells of the immune system.
Cytotoxic T cells engulf bacteria by phagocytosis and digest them internally.
Both B and T lymphocytes complete their maturation in the thymus.
questions.exp: B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow and, when activated, give rise to plasma cells that secrete antibodies. T lymphocytes mature in the thymus; cytotoxic T cells recognise and kill infected host cells by contact. Phagocytosis of bacteria is carried out by macrophages and neutrophils.

questions.stem: Which statement about the cytoskeleton is correct?
options: Microtubules are hollow polymers of tubulin that form the mitotic spindle and the core of cilia and flagella.
Microfilaments are hollow tubes of tubulin that give cilia their characteristic internal arrangement.
The contractile ring that divides an animal cell during cytokinesis is made of microtubules.
Microtubules are permanently fixed structures that never assemble or disassemble inside the cell.
Actin microfilaments form the spindle fibres that separate chromosomes during mitosis.
questions.exp: Microtubules, built of tubulin, form the mitotic spindle, the axoneme of cilia and flagella, and rails for intracellular transport. Microfilaments of actin support cell shape, power muscle contraction and form the cleavage furrow of cytokinesis. The cytoskeleton is dynamic and constantly remodeled.

questions.stem: Which statement about apoptosis is correct?
options: Apoptosis is the uncontrolled death of cells after injury, and it always triggers inflammation.
Cells dying by apoptosis release their digestive enzymes into the surrounding tissue.
Apoptosis is a genetically regulated process in which the cell is dismantled into fragments that nearby cells engulf without causing inflammation.
Apoptosis plays no role in healthy embryonic development.
Apoptosis is triggered only by external toxins and never by signals arising within the cell itself.
questions.exp: Apoptosis is programmed cell death: internal or external signals activate genes and enzymes that neatly break the cell into fragments, which are phagocytosed without inflammation. It also shapes normal development, for example removing the webbing between developing fingers. The descriptions in the other options fit necrosis.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly matches a level of protein structure with what defines it?
options: The primary structure is defined by hydrogen bonding between atoms of the polypeptide backbone.
The secondary structure is defined by disulfide bridges between cysteine residues.
The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids joined together by peptide bonds.
The tertiary structure is the assembly of several separate polypeptide chains into one functional unit.
The quaternary structure is the local coiling of the chain into alpha helices.
questions.exp: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, linked by covalent peptide bonds. Secondary structure (alpha helices and beta sheets) is held by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups, tertiary structure is the overall three dimensional fold stabilised by interactions including disulfide bridges, and quaternary structure is the joining of multiple polypeptide chains.

questions.stem: A person standing outside in cold weather starts to shiver. Which statement about this response is correct?
options: Skin blood vessels widen so that warm blood flows close to the surface, warming the skin.
Sweat production increases so that evaporation can release heat from the body core.
Shivering is involuntary contraction of skeletal muscles that generates heat, coordinated by the hypothalamus as part of a negative feedback response to falling body temperature.
Shivering is a voluntary response that the person chooses to start in order to warm up.
Shivering cools the body further, because the contracting muscles push warm blood to the skin surface where heat is lost.
questions.exp: Cold is detected and the hypothalamus responds with vasoconstriction of skin arterioles, reduced sweating and shivering. Shivering is rapid involuntary skeletal muscle contraction that releases heat as the muscle fibres work, and together these negative feedback responses counteract the fall in core temperature.
